item.content:encoded:
Researchers demonstrated autonomous AI systems that spontaneously share knowledge to accelerate materials discovery. Meanwhile, scientists developed rare-earth-free magnets using abundant elements, and new AI tools are making molecular design 10x faster.

AI Systems Learn to Collaborate

A joint research team from NIMS and the University of Tsukuba developed autonomous AI network technology that enables multiple AI systems to spontaneously collaborate by sharing knowledge for materials discovery. In simulations, three AI systems exchanged knowledge and improved optimization speed through this spontaneous collaboration.

The technology mimics how human researchers communicate and share insights across labs. Rather than working in isolation, the AI systems transfer learned knowledge to each other, accelerating the exploration of materials space. The team published their findings in npj Computational Materials in December 2025.

This approach addresses a key bottleneck in computational materials discovery: each AI system typically starts from scratch, even when similar problems have been solved elsewhere. By enabling knowledge transfer between autonomous systems, the technology could accelerate the discovery and synthesis of new materials across distributed research networks.

Materials Breakthroughs

Rare-Earth-Free Magnets

Researchers at Georgetown University discovered a new class of strong magnets based on high-entropy borides that use only earth-abundant transition metals and boron. The materials exhibit high magnetic anisotropy , a key property for permanent magnets, without requiring rare-earth elements.

The team synthesized the materials using a combinatorial sputtering method that enables rapid testing of multiple compositions simultaneously—up to 50 samples on a single substrate. The high-entropy approach combines five or more elements in near-equal proportions, creating materials with properties distinct from conventional alloys.

This work opens pathways toward sustainable magnetic technologies for motors, MRI machines, and data storage. The research was published in Advanced Materials in 2025.

Robust Crystalline Sponge

The Institute of Science Tokyo developed APF-80 , a robust metal-organic framework (MOF) for the crystalline sponge method used in molecular structure analysis. Previous MOFs were too fragile for practical use, limiting the technique’s application.

APF-80 overcomes these fragility issues , enabling structural elucidation of complex, reactive molecules like alkaloids from minute quantities. The method works by absorbing target molecules into the MOF’s pores, where they can be analyzed via X-ray diffraction without requiring crystallization of the molecule itself.

This advancement is expected to accelerate pharmaceutical research by enabling structure determination of compounds that are difficult to crystallize or available only in small amounts.

New Quantum State

Physicists from Rice University and Vienna University of Technology discovered a topological semimetal phase in CeRu4Sn6 at near absolute zero temperature. The state emerged through quantum criticality and was identified via an unusual Hall effect without an external magnetic field.

The finding challenges previous assumptions: strong electron interactions can create, not destroy, topological states . This insight could inform advances in quantum computing, electronic efficiencies, and sensing technologies by revealing new mechanisms for engineering topological quantum materials.

Material Key Property Significance
High-entropy borides High magnetic anisotropy Rare-earth-free magnets
APF-80 MOF Robust structure Drug discovery tool
CeRu4Sn6 Topological semimetal phase Quantum applications

AI Tools Accelerate Discovery

Faster Molecular Design

Researchers from NYU and the University of Florida developed PropMolFlow , an AI model that designs molecules with specified properties 10 times faster than previous methods. The system reduces computational steps from 1,000 to 100 while maintaining 90% accuracy for generating chemically valid structures.

The method works backward from desired properties to molecular structures, validated using physics-based density functional theory. This “inverse design” approach accelerates discovery for pharmaceuticals and materials by directly targeting specific characteristics rather than screening large libraries. The work was published in Nature Computational Science in January 2026.

Human-AI Collaboration

Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago developed an AI advisor model for autonomous labs that enables collaborative decision-making between humans and AI. Applied to the Polybot self-driving lab, the system created a mixed ion-electron conducting polymer with a 150% performance improvement over previous methods.

The approach combines human expertise with AI’s data-processing capabilities, allowing researchers to guide autonomous experiments while leveraging machine learning for optimization. The team published their findings in Nature Chemical Engineering in December 2025.

Quantum Machine Learning

Researchers from the University of Maryland and IonQ demonstrated that quantum kernel machine learning outperforms classical methods in navigating materials phase space using less experimental data. The study, conducted on IonQ’s Aria trapped-ion quantum computer, used X-ray diffraction patterns from an Fe-Ga-Pd alloy library.

The work provides experimental evidence for quantum advantage in materials discovery, particularly when working with complex diffraction data and limited experimental samples . The findings suggest quantum computing could accelerate autonomous experimentation in materials science.

Method Key Metric Application
Autonomous AI Network 3 systems collaborated Materials optimization
PropMolFlow 10x faster, 100 steps Molecular design
AI Advisor 150% performance gain Autonomous labs
Quantum Kernel ML Less data needed Phase space navigation

Data Infrastructure

NIMS developed Research Data Express (RDE) , a flexible data management system designed to standardize and automate materials science data processing. Since its 2023 launch, the platform has seen significant adoption: 5,000 users , 1,900 Dataset Templates implemented, 16,000 datasets created, and 3 million accumulated data files .

RDE uses customizable Dataset Templates to interpret data from various experiments, reducing researchers’ data processing burden and promoting FAIR data principles. The system serves as key infrastructure for Japan’s national materials science initiatives, addressing the critical bottleneck of inconsistent and siloed data that hampers collaborative research and AI-driven discovery.

Funding and Industry Moves

TU/e secured $1.5 million euros as part of the $6 million euro Horizon Europe project SimuLingua, which aims to develop a next-generation AI platform for materials discovery. The project will create a multimodal scientific foundation model enabling researchers to explore materials via natural language and AI-accelerated simulations.

Novyte Materials raised pre-seed funding led by Theia Ventures to support its AI-driven materials discovery platform. The company aims to cut R&D time by up to 10x and reduce testing costs by 90%.

South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT announced a $275.4 billion won investment in the 2026 Nano and Materials R&D Project, focusing on securing core materials technologies and integrating AI to accelerate research.

Energy Fuels is acquiring Australian Strategic Materials for approximately $447 million AUD, highlighting strategic moves to secure critical minerals supply chains and reduce dependence on China for rare earth processing.

Also This Week

Pablo Jarillo-Herrero (MIT) and Allan MacDonald (University of Texas) won the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award for their discovery of the “magic angle” in graphene layers. Their work on twistronics—rotating graphene at 1.1 degrees to control electronic properties—has applications in quantum computing and energy-efficient AI.

The Materials Project has been cited 32,000 times and serves 650,000 users, accelerating research in batteries and quantum computing. The platform provides high-throughput computational modeling and AI-ready datasets, with 99.98% uptime on its cloud infrastructure.

This comprehensive review covers 65 articles published during December 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. As the field matures from hype toward measurable progress, researchers proposed standardized KPIs to evaluate quantum systems, silicon-based chips demonstrated record fidelities, and error correction crossed new thresholds globally.

The Big Story: Quantum Computing Seeks Standard Metrics

As quantum computing matures, the field is grappling with a fundamental problem: how to objectively measure progress. In December, researchers proposed key performance indicators (KPIs) to standardize the evaluation of quantum systems, aiming to distinguish genuine breakthroughs from spurious claims. The effort, documented in a 2025 preprint by Lall et al., seeks to provide comparable metrics across different hardware platforms, algorithms, and evaluation methods.

The push for standardization comes as the field grapples with what metrics actually matter. Research published in Nature Communications and elsewhere has shown that stabilizer metrics may only provide an upper bound on quantum performance, not a complete picture of system capability. Meanwhile, researchers have mapped how errors evolve over time in quantum memory systems, providing better context for what reliability claims mean in practice.

Concrete verification methods are also emerging. Scientists at Swinburne University developed techniques to verify the accuracy of Gaussian Boson Sampler (GBS) devices, quickly identifying errors in experiments that would take thousands of years to simulate classically. The method can detect deviations from expected results, a critical capability as quantum systems grow too complex for classical verification.

This focus on measurement reflects a broader shift in the field. As McKinsey noted in a December analysis , quantum leaders and investors are increasingly prioritizing quantum error correction as the critical path to utility, with investment in quantum startups surging 50% in 2024.

Error Correction Breakthroughs

Microwave Control Advances

Chinese researchers achieved a significant milestone in December, demonstrating fault-tolerant quantum error correction using an all-microwave method on a 107-qubit processor. This marks the first time a group outside the US has crossed this key reliability threshold. The team, led by Pan Jianwei from the University of Science and Technology of China, achieved an error-suppression factor of 1.4 with a distance-7 surface-code logical qubit—a scale comparable to Google’s recent advances.

The microwave-based approach offers a practical advantage: it suppresses leakage errors without requiring extra hardware, potentially easing scaling bottlenecks. As reported in Physical Review Letters , the method tackles qubit drift and error propagation more efficiently than hardware-intensive approaches.

Complementary research from the same team demonstrated a new method to fix leakage errors using targeted microwave pulses . Tested on a 97-qubit processor, the technique suppressed leakage errors over 70 times more effectively than running without suppression. Critically, the system became more reliable as more qubits were added—a key requirement for scalable quantum computing.

Hardware Solutions

European researchers achieved a breakthrough in superconducting qubit control, developing analytical formulas called R1D and R2D that achieve gate fidelities of 99.999% for rapid X-gate rotations. The work from Forschungszentrum Jülich, University of Cologne, and RWTH Aachen University addresses limitations in qubit control under strong driving, providing a blueprint for more reliable quantum processors.

On the decoding side, Riverlane published a peer-reviewed paper in Nature Communications detailing its Local Clustering Decoder (LCD), a hardware decoder that achieves real-time quantum error correction for the surface code. The decoder breaks the traditional trade-off between speed and accuracy, performing one round in under a microsecond and adapting to changing noise conditions. It forms the core of Riverlane’s Deltaflow stack and has been deployed on systems from partners including Infleqtion and Rigetti Computing.

Silicon Chips Show Record Fidelities

Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) published breakthrough results in Nature in December, demonstrating an 11-qubit quantum processor in silicon that achieves fidelity rates between 99.5% and 99.99% . The processor uses a novel “14/15” architecture that places phosphorus atoms in silicon with atomic precision, achieving feature sizes of just 0.13 nanometers.

The significance of this work goes beyond the numbers. As SQC’s research shows, their silicon-based processor scales without losing fidelity —qubit quality actually improves as qubit count increases, contrary to typical quantum systems. The architecture demonstrates atomic, silicon-based quantum computing across separate clusters for the first time, with multi-register linkages maintaining fidelities above fault-tolerance benchmarks.

This modular approach addresses what SQC calls the key quantum scaling problem : how to connect qubit registers while preserving high gate fidelities. The company’s proprietary atomic-scale manufacturing process, developed over 25 years, allows it to produce its own quantum chips with 0.13 nanometer precision.

On the commercialization front, SEALSQ announced a CMOS-compatible roadmap targeting quantum processor production from 2026 to 2030, positioning silicon-based approaches as a potentially manufacturable path to scale.

Capital Moves: Quantum Art $100M, Government Investments

Private Funding

Quantum Art closed a $100 million Series A funding round to scale its multi-core trapped-ion quantum computers, bringing total funding to $124 million. The round, one of the largest for trapped-ion systems, will accelerate development of the company’s 1,000-qubit Perspective system and prototyping of a third-generation architecture targeting thousands of qubits. The company also demonstrated a 200-ion chain and collaborations with NVIDIA and Ayalon Highways.

Nu Quantum raised $60 million in Series A funding , the largest financing round for quantum computer networking. The Cambridge-based company is developing quantum networking technology to enable distributed quantum computing.

QubitSolve secured a $1.2 million NSF SBIR Phase II grant to accelerate development of its quantum computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software. The Morgantown-based startup is transitioning from a 2D prototype to a 3D minimum viable product, with commercial release targeted for late 2027.

Government Investment

Canada launched the Canadian Quantum Champions Program, allocating up to $92 million in initial public funding to four domestic quantum firms—Anyon Systems, Nord Quantique, Photonic, and Xanadu Quantum Technologies. This Phase 1 initiative is part of a broader $334.3 million investment from Budget 2025 aimed at strengthening Canada’s quantum ecosystem and developing fault-tolerant quantum computers.

The Oak Ridge Quantum Science Center secured $125 million in DOE funding for its 2025-2030 program, focusing on quantum materials research and joined-up, multidisciplinary approaches to quantum challenges.

Fujitsu announced a $100,000 quantum simulator challenge , inviting researchers to tackle real-world problems using its 40-qubit quantum simulator.

Company Amount Type Focus
Quantum Art $100M Series A Trapped-ion systems
Nu Quantum $60M Series A Quantum networking
Canada Champions $92M Government 4 domestic firms
Oak Ridge QSC $125M DOE funding 2025-30 program

Global Quantum Deployments Accelerate

Europe

Spain’s CESGA selected IQM Quantum Computers and Telefónica to deploy two on-premises quantum computers: a 54-qubit IQM Radiance system and a 5-qubit IQM Spark for education. Scheduled for delivery by June 2026, this marks Spain’s first quantum-HPC integration and IQM’s first installation in the country.

In Germany, Universal Quantum and Atlas Copco partnered to co-develop industrial-grade vacuum systems for scalable trapped-ion quantum computers. The collaboration aims to transition vacuum technology from laboratory tools to integrated solutions for modular quantum architectures.

FullStaQD announced a new quantum software stack to optimize quantum application development, part of broader European efforts to build complete quantum computing ecosystems.

Qilimanjaro and Oxigen Data Center partnered on multimodal quantum-HPC integration, enabling hybrid quantum-classical workflows for Spanish researchers.

Asia-Pacific & Middle East

Israel’s Quantum Computing Center (IQCC) deployed Qolab’s scalable superconducting qubit device , marking the first installation of the Nobel laureate-founded company’s hardware outside its US lab. The device uses Quantum Machines’ control technology and will be available via cloud access.

Chile launched a National Quantum Strategy 2025-2035 , prioritizing sovereign capabilities in quantum computing, sensing, and communications. The strategy aims to transition Chile to a knowledge-based economy with applications in mining, energy, and telecommunications.

India’s Andhra Pradesh unveiled a Quantum Vision plan to establish Amaravati as a global quantum computing hub among the world’s top five. The initiative targets local quantum computer production within two years and includes a Rs 100-crore (approximately $12 million) Nobel Prize award for quantum research.

In Singapore, Keysight Technologies entered a five-year collaboration with A*STAR, NUS, and NTU to co-develop scalable qubit control architectures, integrating digital control systems with novel processor architectures.

Xanadu expanded its partnership with A*STAR to advance photonic quantum computing, strengthening Singapore’s position in the quantum landscape.

The UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre partnered with Google to give UK researchers access to Google’s advanced Willow quantum chip through an open competition, aiming to uncover new real-world applications in chemistry and medicine.

Location System Qubits Timeline Partner
Spain (CESGA) IQM Radiance 54 By June 2026 IQM, Telefónica
Israel (IQCC) Qolab Scalable Deployed Qolab, Quantum Machines
Chile National Strategy N/A 2025-2035 Government-led

Research Roundup: Optical Chips, Algorithms, and Applications

Optical Advances

Researchers developed a tiny optical phase modulator nearly 100 times smaller than a human hair that uses 80 times less microwave power than commercial modulators. The device, from University of Colorado at Boulder and Sandia National Laboratories, uses microwave-frequency vibrations to manipulate laser light and is manufactured using scalable CMOS fabrication. This breakthrough could enable control of thousands or millions of qubits for trapped-ion and trapped-neutral-atom quantum computers.

Multiple publications highlighted the significance of this work. As reported in ScienceDaily , the chip oscillates billions of times per second and is aimed at the critical bottleneck of optical control for scaling quantum computers. Stanford University researchers separately demonstrated room-temperature quantum communication using molybdenum diselenide and silicon nanostructures, potentially enabling low-cost quantum technologies without extreme cooling.

Algorithms & Software

Researchers developed CircPack, a framework for parallel execution of quantum circuits on trapped-ion computers that treats circuit scheduling as a packing problem. The framework achieves up to 70.72% higher fidelity, 62.67% better utilization, and 32.80% improved layer reduction compared to existing methods, enhancing quantum cloud computing efficiency.

Nature Communications published research on AI integration into the quantum stack, demonstrating how machine learning can optimize quantum operations.

Neutral-Atom Progress

Researchers at Xiangtan University trapped 2,400 Ytterbium-174 atoms in an optical tweezer array with 83.5% loading efficiency, a significant improvement in scalability for quantum computing. The achievement, using optimized laser cooling and real-time feedback, paves the way for larger quantum systems with estimated two-qubit gate fidelities of 99.9%.

Atom Computing developed a method for “qubit recycling” , replenishing atoms from a separate trap to reduce errors and atom loss in neutral-atom quantum computers. Published in Physical Review X, the work enables more complex and longer quantum circuits.

Russian researchers from Lomonosov Moscow State University tested a 72-qubit quantum computer based on neutral rubidium atoms, achieving 94% accuracy in two-qubit operations. The system uses a three-zone architecture for computation, storage, and readout, with plans to reach several hundred high-fidelity qubits by 2030.

Applications

Xanadu published a quantum computational framework demonstrating how fault-tolerant quantum computers can model photosensitizers for photodynamic cancer therapy. The research provides resource estimates for utility-scale hardware and projects significant runtime reductions for classical simulation bottlenecks. The announcement coincided with Xanadu’s planned business combination expected to provide approximately $500 million in capital.

Researchers from IBM, RIKEN, Google, and Quantinuum demonstrated progress in applying quantum computers to chemistry problems throughout 2025 . Qunova Computing reported a quantum algorithm achieving 10 times the efficiency of traditional methods for chemistry calculations.

Nature published research on quantum computing methods for materials simulation, expanding the range of applications for near-term quantum hardware.

Networked Systems

IonQ published a study finding that linked quantum computers can outperform larger single systems. The research suggests a modular approach to scaling rather than building monolithic processors.

Japan achieved a milestone in remote quantum computing , enabling cloud-based access to quantum systems across geographical distances.

Industry Briefs

Amazon reorganized its quantum computing efforts , combining AI, silicon, and quantum computing under a unified structure to streamline development and resource allocation.

Microsoft’s Majorana 1 quantum computer chip continued to generate discussion and controversy . The chip relies on unproven topological qubits based on Majorana zero modes, with some experts remaining unconvinced by the data. Microsoft’s project advanced to the final phase of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative.

IonQ highlighted the historical significance of Dr. Chris Monroe’s 1995 quantum logic gate , which marked the practical birth of quantum computing. The company, founded in 2015, now targets 80,000 logical qubits by 2030 and recently announced a world-record 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity.

IBM announced expansion of its Quantum program in Poughkeepsie, New York, planning to build the world’s first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2033 via its Starling (2029) and Bluejay (2033) projects. The expansion is part of IBM’s broader $1 billion investment in quantum services.

Quantum Computing Inc. agreed to acquire Luminar Semiconductor for $110 million in an all-cash transaction, bringing photonic technologies, patents, and talent to accelerate its quantum systems roadmap.

D-Wave announced it will showcase its quantum computing technology at CES 2026, highlighting real-world customer success stories and applications.

The telecom industry is preparing for quantum computing’s impact by enhancing network security with quantum-safe technologies like post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD). Companies including Orange Business, Telefónica, and Nokia are offering solutions and exploring quantum computing for network optimization.

MOTH, a quantum technology company, announced that quantum computing can overcome classical computing limits in game development, introducing Archaeo, a hardware-agnostic quantum platform for creative workflows, and highlighting Space Moths, a multiplayer game that uses quantum computers to generate levels in real time.

Looking Ahead to 2026

The developments of December 2025 point to a field maturing toward practical applications. Microsoft has introduced a three-level framework for quantum computing progress , with level-two error-corrected machines set for delivery in 2026. These machines, built by Microsoft with Atom Computing and by QuEra, use neutral atoms as qubits for improved scalability and error correction.

The partnership between Microsoft and Atom Computing will deliver the Magne machine with 50 logical qubits and 1,200 physical qubits by the start of 2027. QuEra’s machine at AIST will feature 37 logical qubits across 260 physical qubits. These systems mark the transition from NISQ-era devices to the first generation of error-corrected quantum computers.

McKinsey’s analysis emphasizes that quantum error correction is the priority for capturing value from quantum technologies, which could generate between $0.9 trillion and $2.0 trillion by 2035. The firm notes that quantum start-up investments were 50% higher in 2024 than 2023, with the market projected to reach nearly $100 billion by 2035.

Looking at 2025 investment trends, The Quantum Insider reports a shift away from broad experimentation toward more targeted bets on trapped-ion and photonic hardware architectures, cloud-accessible quantum software platforms, and quantum security technologies. Individual funding rounds for trapped-ion and photonic quantum computer companies reached the $1 billion range.

IBM’s roadmap targets fully error-corrected quantum machines by 2029 , with large-scale systems capable of 1 billion quantum operations by 2029 and 1 billion operations by 2033. The company positions the Hudson Valley as “Quantum Valley,” building on its history of mainframe computing innovation.

As the University of Oxford’s new Quantum Institute Director Ian Walmsley noted , the field is setting the agenda for the next century of quantum science, with deep expertise and cross-disciplinary collaboration accelerating impact across computing, communications, and sensing.

item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published between September 1-30, 2025, surveying a month that fundamentally altered the quantum computing landscape. Caltech built a 6,100-qubit processor (5x the previous record). PsiQuantum raised $1 billion in a single round. Nvidia made three major strategic investments in quantum companies. HSBC ran the world’s first quantum-enabled bond trading. And quantum computers are now being manufactured in standard silicon chip foundries.

The Record Breaker

On September 25, Caltech physicists led by Professor Manuel Endres unveiled the largest qubit array ever assembled : a 6,100-qubit neutral-atom processor that shatters the previous record of 1,180 qubits held by Atom Computing by a factor of five. The achievement, published in Nature , represents a genuine leap forward for scalable quantum computing.

The Caltech array achieves both scale and quality: qubits maintain superposition for 13 seconds with 99.98% manipulation accuracy. The system uses 12,000 optical tweezers to trap individual cesium atoms, arranged in a 1.5mm diameter field of view with 7.2 micrometer spacing between atoms. The coherence time is 10 times longer than previous arrays, and the system can continuously reload atoms at a rate of 300,000 atoms per second while maintaining quantum information.

The breakthrough matters because neutral-atom quantum computing has emerged as one of the most promising paths to large-scale quantum processors. Unlike superconducting qubits, which require expensive dilution refrigerators and complex wiring, neutral atoms can be manipulated at room temperature and reconfigured dynamically using optical tweezers. This flexibility enables “zone-based” quantum computing architectures where qubits can be shuffled between computation, memory, and measurement regions.

Researchers believe this approach can scale to a million qubits within a decade . The Caltech team achieved 99.99% imaging fidelity and 99.98% single-qubit gate fidelity, with loading probabilities exceeding 51% per site. The array uses 11,998 tweezer sites to trap and manipulate the 6,100 active qubits.

The record-breaking system demonstrates that neutral-atom quantum computing can achieve both scale and quality simultaneously—two requirements typically in tension. Previous approaches either achieved high qubit counts with poor coherence, or excellent coherence with limited qubit numbers. Caltech’s system delivers both: room-temperature trapping lifetimes of 23 minutes and coherent transport distances of 610 micrometers with 99.95% transport fidelity.

This advancement comes alongside progress from Harvard, MIT, and QuEra, who demonstrated a 3,000-qubit system capable of continuous operation for over two hours by solving the “atom loss” problem using optical lattice conveyor belts. The Harvard system reloaded 50 million atoms over two hours while maintaining quantum information.

Together, these achievements demonstrate that multiple hardware modalities are making rapid progress. Neutral atoms, superconducting circuits, trapped ions, and silicon spin qubits are all advancing toward the threshold of error-corrected quantum computing. The question is no longer whether any single approach will win—it’s which problems each modality will solve best.

The $2.5 Billion Month

September 2025 will be remembered as the month quantum computing funding went mainstream. Three companies raised over $1.9 billion in private capital, achieving valuations that rival established technology companies. But the more significant signal may be NVIDIA’s strategic pivot: after years of skepticism, the GPU giant made three major quantum investments in a single month.

The Three Giants

PsiQuantum led the fundraising parade with a $1 billion Series E that values the company at $7 billion . The round, led by BlackRock, Temasek, and Baillie Gifford, included strategic investment from NVIDIA’s venture arm. The capital will fund construction of utility-scale quantum computing sites in Brisbane and Chicago, targeting a 2027 operational date for the Brisbane system. PsiQuantum’s photonic approach aims to build million-qubit systems using semiconductor manufacturing processes.

Quantinuum, the Honeywell-controlled trapped-ion leader, secured $600 million in equity funding at a $10 billion pre-money valuation. New investors included Quanta Computer, NVIDIA’s NVentures, and QED Investors. The funding will support the 2025 launch of the Helios quantum computer and progress toward the Apollo fault-tolerant system planned for 2029. Quantinuum also announced selection for DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, targeting utility-scale quantum computing by 2033.

IQM, the European superconducting quantum startup, raised $320 million in Series B funding achieving unicorn status with a $1 billion valuation. The company, founded in 2018, has sold 15 quantum computers and plans to use the funds for global expansion and software platform development. The round highlights growing European investor interest in quantum technology—currently, the EU accounts for only 5% of global private quantum funding compared to 50% for the United States.

Infleqtion announced a SPAC deal valuing the neutral-atom quantum computing firm at $1.8 billion , targeting $540 million in proceeds. The company also unveiled a new architecture accelerating its roadmap to 1,000 logical qubits by 2030.

NVIDIA’s Quantum Bet

The most significant strategic signal in September came from NVIDIA. After years of observing quantum computing from the sidelines, the company made three major quantum investments : PsiQuantum, Quantinuum, and an expanded partnership developing GPU-accelerated quantum simulation tools.

NVIDIA’s shift is telling. The company that powers the AI revolution is now betting that quantum computing will be a complementary technology for solving certain classes of problems. The company’s research collaborations achieved 50x speedups in error correction decoding and 4,000x performance boosts in quantum simulation, demonstrating that classical computing and quantum computing will advance in tandem.

The Government Wave

Public investment surged alongside private capital. New York State announced $300 million for a quantum hub at Stony Brook University. New Mexico committed $315 million to quantum computing initiatives. The National Science Foundation awarded $16 million for the design phase of the National Quantum Virtual Laboratory, including $4 million for a University of New Mexico-led team designing photonic quantum computers.

New Mexico partnered with DARPA to invest up to $240 million over four years in the Quantum Frontier Project, leveraging Sandia and Los Alamos national laboratories. The Maryland Quantum-Thermodynamics Hub secured over $5 million in combined state and private funding.

Hardware: Multiple Paths Forward

While NVIDIA’s quantum investments validate the industry’s commercial prospects, the hardware advances in September demonstrate that multiple technical paths are advancing in parallel. Quantum computing hardware progressed across all major modalities, with each approach solving different pieces of the scaling puzzle. The field is converging on a realization: different quantum computing technologies will likely serve different applications rather than a single winner-take-all outcome.

Modular & Superconducting

University of Illinois researchers developed modular quantum computers that “snap together like LEGO bricks” using superconducting qubits and coaxial cables. The system achieved approximately 99% SWAP gate fidelity, enabling scalable, reconfigurable architectures. Modular approaches address a fundamental challenge in quantum computing: as systems grow larger, the complexity of connecting all qubits becomes unmanageable. By building smaller modules and linking them, researchers can maintain high gate fidelities while scaling.

UC Berkeley and Northwestern scientists demonstrated a superconducting “grid states” qubit that intrinsically protects quantum information from decoherence. By integrating a Cooper-quartet junction with a phase-slip element in a high-impedance circuit, the team created robust qubit states that offer an alternative to active error correction.

Trapped Ion & Neutral Atom

Trapped-ion systems achieved what researchers call “unconditional quantum supremacy.” UT Austin and Quantinuum researchers proved that a 12-qubit quantum computer can complete a memory storage task that would require 62 to 382 bits of classical memory. This “quantum information supremacy” is permanent—no future classical algorithm or hardware improvement can close the gap because the result follows from information theory rather than computational complexity.

Neutral-atom systems continued their rapid advancement. Beyond Caltech’s record 6,100-qubit array, Harvard/MIT/QuEra researchers solved the atom loss problem that has limited continuous operation. Their 3,000-qubit system ran for over two hours by using optical lattice conveyor belts to rapidly resupply lost qubits without destroying quantum information. This capability is essential for error-corrected quantum computing, which requires long-duration coherent operations.

Silicon Spin Qubits

Silicon-based quantum computing achieved two breakthroughs in September. UNSW Sydney researchers demonstrated quantum entanglement between two atomic nuclei separated by 20 nanometers using a geometric gate method. The 76% fidelity entanglement allows nuclei to communicate via electrons even when not close together, enabling scaling compatible with standard silicon chip fabrication.

The system uses the hyperfine coupling of 111-113 MHz in phosphorus donors, with 12 MHz Heisenberg exchange interactions between electrons. The 2-microsecond controlled-Z gate operations and 99% nuclei readability demonstrate that silicon spin qubits can achieve the fidelities required for error correction while leveraging existing semiconductor manufacturing.

Researchers achieved 90% fidelity in generating 4-qubit cluster states , a foundational resource for measurement-based quantum computation using superconducting circuits. The study identified that dephasing noise severely degrades cluster states, providing guidance for targeted error-mitigation strategies.

Commercial: Going to Market

September marked a decisive shift from research prototypes to commercial products. Customers are now paying for quantum computers, deploying them in data centers, and using them to solve business problems.

Performance Milestones

IonQ announced its Tempo quantum computer achieved an algorithmic qubit (AQ) score of 64 , three months ahead of schedule. The AQ 64 system can access over 18 quintillion computational states, representing a 268 million-fold increase in computational space from AQ 36. The milestone demonstrates exponential scaling in quantum computing performance, with IonQ showing 35% improvement in QAOA solution quality, 74% improvement in Quantum Fourier Transform implementation, and 182% improvement in quantum search algorithms compared to competing systems.

Algorithmic qubits differ from physical qubits—they represent the effective computational power after accounting for error rates and gate fidelities. IonQ’s AQ 64 achievement suggests the company is on track toward its goal of 2 million qubits by 2030.

First Deployments

Commercial deployments accelerated geographically. Rigetti Computing announced approximately $5.7 million in purchase orders for two of its 9-qubit Novera quantum computing systems. One is destined for an Asian tech manufacturer developing internal expertise, the other for a California-based startup researching hardware and error correction. Both systems are upgradeable and expected for delivery in the first half of 2026.

Oxford Quantum Circuits installed New York City’s first quantum computer at a Digital Realty Trust data center in Manhattan. The British startup plans to spend tens of millions of dollars over three to five years integrating NVIDIA chips into the system, aiming to run AI programs more efficiently.

Czechia launched its first public quantum computer, VLK, at the IT4Innovations National Supercomputing Center in Ostrava. Built with 125 million Czech crowns in EU support, it is the second publicly available quantum computer in Europe. The system operates at close to -273 degrees Celsius and will be used for atmospheric monitoring research with the European Space Agency.

Manufacturing Breakthrough

The most significant commercial development came from Quantum Motion, which delivered the industry’s first full-stack silicon CMOS quantum computer to the UK National Quantum Computing Centre. The system uses standard 300mm silicon chip manufacturing—the same process used for conventional electronics—fitting into three 19-inch server racks.

The deployment demonstrates that quantum computers can be built using established, mass-producible semiconductor infrastructure. The system uses a modular “tile” architecture designed to scale to millions of qubits and is compatible with Qiskit and Cirq software frameworks. With two-qubit gate fidelities reaching 98% in prior research, silicon spin qubits are approaching the error-correction threshold while leveraging decades of manufacturing investment.

Quantum Motion’s system represents a cost-effective path to scaling because it uses existing chip fabs rather than requiring specialized manufacturing. The company’s architecture aims for millions of qubits per quantum processing unit, with a goal of 1 trillion quantum operations in error-corrected systems by 2035.

Applications: Solving Real Problems

Beyond hardware advances, September demonstrated that quantum computers are increasingly being applied to concrete challenges across finance, healthcare, and fundamental science.

Finance & Trading

HSBC, working with IBM, delivered the world’s first-known quantum-enabled algorithmic trading trial using real production-scale data from the European corporate bond market. The integration of IBM’s Heron quantum processor with classical systems achieved up to 34% improvement in predicting winning trades compared to classical methods alone.

The trial marks a practical step for quantum computing in financial applications, demonstrating that hybrid quantum-classical approaches can provide competitive advantages in algorithmic trading. HSBC used the system for bond price prediction, addressing one of the most liquid and complex markets in global finance.

Healthcare & Drug Discovery

SciSparc Ltd. announced an initiative to advance 3D protein modeling using quantum computing technology. The program aims to transform drug discovery by achieving unprecedented accuracy in predicting protein structures and interactions, targeting neurological and rare diseases.

University of Saskatchewan researchers are using quantum computers to simulate pathogens and test vaccine scenarios, aiming to produce vaccines in less than 100 days from the start of a new pandemic. The work partners the university’s quantum research center (quanTA) with the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization (VIDO), funded in part by federal grants and IBM Quantum Division access.

The research aims to radically shorten pandemic response times by using quantum simulation to model pathogen behavior and vaccine interactions. Their goal of sub-100-day vaccine development would represent a dramatic acceleration compared to traditional timelines.

Algorithmic Breakthroughs

Google Quantum AI researchers demonstrated “generative quantum advantage” for the first time , showing quantum computers can learn to generate outputs—like complex bitstrings or compressed circuits—that classical systems cannot replicate. The team used a 68-qubit superconducting processor and “instantaneously deep quantum neural networks” trained via a “sewing technique” to overcome optimization roadblocks.

The work moves quantum advantage beyond simple sampling toward trainable generative tasks, with potential applications in materials science and circuit optimization. The effective qubit count reached 816 in performance evaluations, with projections that 34,000 qubits would exceed classical reach.

Los Alamos National Laboratory and IBM researchers used a quantum algorithm to solve the century-old mathematical problem of factoring group representations, which was intractable for classical computers. The algorithm employs quantum Fourier transforms and has direct applications in particle physics, material science, and data transmission.

Partnerships: Building the Ecosystem

Big Tech Moves

Microsoft announced a new quantum research center at the University of Maryland’s Discovery District, featuring a prototype of Microsoft’s topological quantum computer. The center will serve as a hub for collaboration with government, academia, and industry, coinciding with Microsoft’s selection for the final phase of DARPA’s US2QC program.

NVIDIA expanded its quantum partnerships, with research achieving 2x speed improvements in quantum error correction decoding , 50x boosts in AI-powered decoders, and 4,000x performance improvements in quantum simulation methods. These advances in classical computing are critical for developing practical quantum applications.

Cisco Quantum Labs announced a unified quantum networking software stack and three research prototypes enabling distributed quantum computing across networked processors. The software includes a quantum compiler for partitioning circuits across multiple quantum computers and classical applications for eavesdropper detection and decision coordination. The company’s quantum network entanglement chip generates over 200 million entangled photon pairs per second.

Government & Academia

Government funding accelerated through multiple channels. The National Science Foundation selected four teams for the design phase of the National Quantum Virtual Laboratory, investing $16 million to provide researchers with shareable quantum computers and digital twins for testing algorithms.

New York State committed $300 million for a Quantum Research and Innovation Hub at Stony Brook University, leveraging Brookhaven National Laboratory and the university’s existing 170-mile quantum computing network. The hub aims to establish Long Island as a major quantum computing center.

New Mexico partnered with DARPA on the Quantum Frontier Project, investing up to $120 million each over four years to make large-scale quantum computers a reality by 2033. The initiative will leverage Sandia and Los Alamos national laboratories.

Global Expansion

QUDORA and Seoul-based Norma Inc. formed a strategic partnership to drive trapped-ion quantum computing adoption across South Korea’s ecosystem, targeting semiconductors and advanced manufacturing industries.

Rigetti Computing and India’s Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) signed an MOU to co-develop hybrid quantum computing systems , combining Rigetti’s superconducting technology with C-DAC’s high-performance computing expertise.

Qilimanjaro and Qblox expanded their collaboration to advance hybrid digital-analog quantum computing in Europe, integrating analog processors with digital superconducting systems at a new Barcelona data center opening in November.

Research: Theoretical Foundations

Error Correction & Noise

IBM Quantum researchers published a study challenging quantum’s “noise barrier” , showing that nonunital noise can be harnessed to extend computations beyond previous theoretical limits. Their “RESET” protocol uses this noise and ancillary qubits to correct errors without mid-circuit measurements, potentially enabling more powerful near-term devices.

The work challenges the prevailing view that noise is purely detrimental, suggesting current noisy processors may be more computationally capable than believed. By harnessing rather than fighting noise, IBM’s approach could accelerate the path to practical quantum advantage.

Researchers achieved 90% fidelity in generating 4-qubit cluster states , identifying that dephasing noise severely degrades cluster states while energy relaxation causes only modest fidelity loss. This insight enables targeted error-mitigation strategies for near-term devices.

Validation & Verification

UT Austin and Quantinuum researchers demonstrated unconditional quantum supremacy, proving that a 12-qubit system can complete a memory storage task that would require 62 to 382 bits of classical memory. This “quantum information supremacy” is the first that cannot be closed by future classical algorithm or hardware improvements because it derives from information theory rather than computational complexity.

Swinburne University researchers developed methods to validate outputs of Gaussian Boson Sampler quantum computers, which solve problems that would take 9,000 years on supercomputers. The team validated a GBS experiment and found errors requiring further investigation, aiming to ensure quantum computers retain their “quantumness” for commercial applications.

Theory & Materials

Perimeter Institute researchers provided a blueprint for understanding quantum computer speed limits by directly linking computational problem complexity to required quantum entanglement. The hardest problems require creating and manipulating highly complex webs of entanglement, which sets fundamental speed limits for quantum computation.

Japanese researchers observed “heavy fermions”—electrons with enhanced mass—exhibiting quantum entanglement governed by Planckian time in the material CeRhSn. The discovery suggests such entangled states in solid-state materials could be harnessed for novel quantum computing architectures.

Utah State University mathematicians developed non-semisimple topological quantum field theories predicting new quantum particles called “neglectons” that may offer more stable qubits, reducing errors from environmental noise.

Emerging Technologies & Infrastructure

Supporting technologies advanced alongside quantum processors, addressing critical bottlenecks in scaling.

Qubic, a Canadian startup, developed a cryogenic traveling-wave parametric amplifier that reduces quantum computer heat emissions by a factor of 10,000. The innovation virtually eliminates heat loss from a key component, potentially reducing running costs and removing a major barrier to scalable quantum systems. The company plans to bring the amplifier to market in 2026.

Quantum Source unveiled ORIGIN, a core engine for scalable photonic quantum computers using Cavity-QED technology to deterministically generate entangled cluster states. The system enables room-temperature quantum computers scaling to millions of qubits, with first product delivery expected by end of 2026.

Delft Circuits announced an I/O roadmap to scale quantum computers to thousands of qubits by addressing connectivity challenges. Their Cri/oFlex cables use superconducting materials to replace coaxial cabling, with projections to increase channel density from 256 to 4,096 channels by 2029.

Quantum Computing Inc. debuted a Quantum Secure Solution using high-dimensional time-energy entangled quantum modes , offering enhanced data density, scalability, and noise resilience. Operating at room temperature, the system integrates with existing telecom infrastructure.

**Maybell Quantum closed a $40 million Series B funding round](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/maybell-quantum-closes-40m-funding-round-for-quantum-computing-fridges/ ) to accelerate commercialization of its cryogenic systems for quantum computing, following a $25 million Series A in March 2024.

Market Signals & Industry Analysis

Financial markets sent strong signals about quantum computing’s commercial trajectory.

Defiance’s QTUM Quantum Computing ETF surpassed $2 billion in assets under management, highlighting growing investor interest in quantum technologies. The ETF, launched in 2018, holds companies like D-Wave Quantum, IonQ, and Rigetti Computing, and carries a 5-star Morningstar Rating.

Analyst firm B. Riley raised IonQ’s 12-month price target to $100, a new street-high reflecting confidence in the company’s path to scalable quantum advantage. IonQ’s stock has gained 805% over the past year, with the company reporting $20.7 million in Q2 2025 revenue (beating expectations by 15%) and forecasting $82-100 million for full year 2025.

A market report projects the global photonic quantum computing market will reach $1.1 billion by 2030 and over $7 billion by 2036, highlighting the rapid growth and commercialization of photonic approaches. The report identifies key advantages including room temperature operation and scalability.

Industry leaders from Fujitsu, Oxford Instruments, Quantinuum, and D-Wave emphasized during a major webinar that quantum computing is transitioning from lab research to commercial applications, with a focus on hybrid systems that complement rather than replace classical computers.

September in Context

September 2025 rewrote the quantum computing record books. The 6,100-qubit Caltech array shattered scaling barriers. Over $2.5 billion in capital flooded into startups, led by PsiQuantum’s $1 billion round and Quantinuum’s $10 billion valuation. NVIDIA made three strategic quantum investments, signaling that the AI and quantum computing paths are converging. HSBC demonstrated the world’s first quantum-enabled bond trading. And quantum computers are now being manufactured in standard silicon chip foundries.

The field is transitioning from scientific curiosity to engineering challenge. Multiple hardware modalities—neutral atoms, superconducting circuits, trapped ions, silicon spin qubits, photonics—are all advancing in parallel. This diversity is strength, not weakness. Different approaches will likely serve different applications: neutral atoms for simulation, trapped ions for algorithms requiring deep circuits, silicon spin qubits for mass deployment, photonics for networking and room-temperature operation.

The question isn’t “if” quantum computers will be useful anymore—it’s “when” and “for what.” NERSC and Berkeley Lab forecast that quantum computers could become practical tools for U.S. Department of Energy scientific workloads within the next decade. IBM’s roadmap targets 200 logical qubits by 2029 and 2,000 logical qubits by 2033. PsiQuantum aims for million-qubit systems by 2027.

But the path remains long. Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires orders of magnitude improvement in qubit quality, error correction, and system integration. September’s achievements demonstrate rapid progress, but the gap between today’s systems and fault-tolerant computers remains substantial.

What changed in September is the perception of quantum computing’s trajectory. The funding surge, commercial deployments, and real-world applications collectively signal that the industry has entered a new phase. The era of laboratory experiments is giving way to commercial deployment. The race is no longer about demonstrating quantum advantage—it’s about delivering quantum utility at scale.

September was extraordinary. But the work ahead is measured in years, not months.

The following table summarizes key company milestones from September 2025:

PsiQuantum $1B Series E $7B valuation, targeting 2027 launch
Quantinuum $600M raise $10B valuation, H2 generation progress
IonQ AQ 64 milestone 3 months ahead of schedule
Quantum Motion Silicon CMOS system First using standard chip fabs
Rigetti $5.7M in orders On-premises commercial deployments
IQM $320M Series B Europe’s largest quantum funding round

item.title: AI Transforms Materials Discovery: From Serendipity to Speed
item.description:
In a single afternoon, researchers discovered a catalyst that replaces expensive iridium for clean hydrogen production. This month, $120 million in funding poured into AI materials startups. Autonomous labs now perform 1,000 experiments daily. The era of slow, accidental materials discovery is ending.

This comprehensive review covers 29 articles published during August 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI-accelerated materials science. High-throughput methods are achieving 10-1000x speed improvements over traditional approaches, autonomous laboratories are moving from research prototypes to commercial facilities, and foundation models trained on billions of molecules are emerging as powerful new tools for materials design.
item.content:encoded:
In a single afternoon, researchers discovered a catalyst that replaces expensive iridium for clean hydrogen production. This month, $120 million in funding poured into AI materials startups. Autonomous labs now perform 1,000 experiments daily. The era of slow, accidental materials discovery is ending.

This comprehensive review covers 29 articles published during August 2025, surveying the latest developments in AI-accelerated materials science. High-throughput methods are achieving 10-1000x speed improvements over traditional approaches, autonomous laboratories are moving from research prototypes to commercial facilities, and foundation models trained on billions of molecules are emerging as powerful new tools for materials design.

The Breakthrough

On August 19, researchers at Northwestern University, in collaboration with the Toyota Research Institute, announced they had discovered a new catalyst for clean hydrogen production—in a single afternoon. The catalyst, made from a combination of four abundant metals, matches or exceeds the performance of iridium for the oxygen evolution reaction while costing just one-sixteenth as much.

This was no accident. The team used a nanomaterial “megalibrary” containing 156 million distinct particles on a single chip. Using machine learning algorithms to analyze the results, they identified a Ru52Co33Mn9Cr6 oxide catalyst that remained stable for 1,000 hours of testing. Iridium currently costs approximately $5,000 per ounce, creating a major barrier to scaling green hydrogen production.

The megalibrary platform, first introduced in 2016, represents a shift from serendipitous discovery to systematic exploration. Rather than testing materials one by one, researchers can now screen millions of compositions in parallel. The Northwestern discovery demonstrates what this approach makes possible: a practical problem (replacing rare iridium) solved in an afternoon instead of years of trial and error.

This speed is becoming characteristic of the field. Professor Toshiaki Taniike at the Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (JAIST) reports that high-throughput experiments combined with machine learning are 10 to 1000 times faster than traditional manual methods. His work on catalysts and polymers uses automatic feature engineering and data science to accelerate discovery, aiming to unlock new chemical reactions like the oxidative coupling of methane for carbon-neutral processes.

The pattern is consistent: materials scientists who once spent months testing hypotheses can now screen thousands of compositions per day, with AI identifying the most promising candidates for human validation.

The Engine: How AI Accelerates Discovery

The acceleration of materials discovery isn’t happening by accident. It’s driven by a convergence of technologies: autonomous laboratories that run experiments continuously, AI foundation models trained on billions of molecules, and closed-loop systems where AI plans experiments and learns from the results in real time.

Autonomous Laboratories

The most visible sign of this transformation is the emergence of self-driving laboratories. On August 25, researchers at North Carolina State University unveiled Rainbow, a multi-robot autonomous laboratory that can perform 1,000 experiments per day and process 96 reactions simultaneously. Rainbow uses AI and robotics to autonomously synthesize and optimize quantum dots for applications in displays, solar cells, and LEDs.

Rainbow is a research platform, but commercial autonomous labs are already operational. Chemify, a spin-out from the University of Glasgow, has opened its first Chemifarm facility—a 21,500 square foot automated lab in Glasgow that uses a chemical programming language and robotics to accelerate drug and materials discovery, according to a report in Technology Networks . The facility represents the first commercial implementation of the “chemputation” platform, which founder Leroy Cronin envisions enabling decentralized manufacturing to address supply chain vulnerabilities. Chemify has grown to 140 employees in just 3.5 years.

Government labs are also open-sourcing their autonomous platforms. NIST announced the Autonomous Formulation Lab (AFL) on August 29, an open-source platform that uses AI-driven robotics to autonomously prepare and test complex fluid mixtures. The system links AI planning with robotic execution and in-situ measurements like small-angle scattering to map phase behavior and optimize formulations for products like paints and vaccines. NIST has made both the code and hardware designs publicly available.

AI Foundation Models

While robotics accelerate the physical work of experimentation, AI foundation models are accelerating the intellectual work of prediction and design. Argonne National Laboratory is using supercomputers to build AI foundation models trained on billions of molecules—a dramatic scale increase from previous models trained on 100 million molecules. The team trained one of the largest chemical foundation models on the Polaris supercomputer in 2024 and is now developing a second model for molecular crystals on the Aurora exascale system.

These foundation models are integrated with chatbots to enable interactive exploration and have already outperformed previous single-property prediction models. The goal is to predict properties for new battery materials including electrolytes and electrodes. Most battery materials in use today were discovered between 1975 and 1985; foundation models could accelerate the discovery of their successors.

At Tohoku University, researchers have developed an AI-built “materials map” using the MatDeepLearn (MDL) framework and message passing neural networks. The map unifies experimental and computational data to visually group structurally similar materials, allowing scientists to quickly identify promising candidates and repurpose existing synthesis protocols. The team demonstrated the approach for thermoelectric materials and plans to extend it to magnetic and topological materials.

Closed-Loop Discovery

The real breakthrough comes when AI planning, robotic execution, and real-time learning are integrated into closed-loop systems. NIST’s AFL exemplifies this approach: AI plans experiments, robots execute them, in-situ measurements provide immediate feedback, and the AI uses those results to plan the next round of experiments. Chemify’s Chemifarm operates on similar principles, with the goal of making chemical discovery and manufacturing a closed-loop, automated process.

Quantum-Integrated Platforms

A new class of platforms is adding quantum computing to the discovery toolkit. On August 19, Mitsui, QSimulate, and Quantinuum launched the QIDO platform , a quantum-integrated chemistry platform that combines classical and quantum computing workflows for high-precision chemical reaction modeling. QIDO integrates QSimulate’s QSP Reaction software with Quantinuum’s InQuanto software, making quantum chemistry technologies more accessible to industrial settings.

What They’re Finding

The accelerated discovery methods are producing results across multiple domains. New materials are emerging for energy storage, electronics, and specialty applications.

Energy Storage

Battery materials research has seen particularly rapid progress. Researchers using a chemical foundation model called SMI-TED have designed new electrolyte formulations for rechargeable batteries. The model, fine-tuned on 13,666 experimental data points, discovered 7 novel formulations that improved ionic conductivity for LiFSI- and LiDFOB-based electrolytes by 82% and 172%, respectively. The workflow is generalizable beyond electrolytes to other chemical mixtures.

At Argonne National Laboratory, foundation models trained on billions of molecules are being applied to discover new materials for both electrolytes and electrodes. Meanwhile, an analysis of the AI-driven battery technology market projects the sector will grow to $19.4 billion by 2034, with a compound annual growth rate of 18.9%. The report notes that AI has identified 500,000 potential new battery materials at Microsoft alone.

Separate research covered by SciTechDaily highlights AI’s role in discovering alternatives to lithium-ion chemistry, including sodium-based and solid-state battery technologies.

Electronics

Next-generation power electronics are another focus of accelerated discovery. Researchers have used high-throughput computational screening to identify new materials for power electronics, screening 153,235 materials from the Materials Project database and identifying 44 promising candidates including B2O3, BeO, and BN. The power electronics market is projected to reach $50 billion by 2025, and approximately 80% of electric power uses power electronics.

Separate computational screening identified novel ultra-wide bandgap semiconductors, with materials like InBO3 showing performance over 6,000 times better than silicon for RF electronics applications. Researchers screened 1,300 potential semiconductor materials using Density Functional Theory and Monte Carlo simulations. These materials could enable more efficient electric vehicle chargers, wireless power transfer, radar systems, and communication devices.

For two-dimensional materials, researchers have developed a substrate-aware computational design method that predicts atomic structure on substrates, combining an evolutionary algorithm, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and lattice-matching. The method discovered new stable and metastable structures in the molybdenum-sulfur system on sapphire substrates and predicts synthesis conditions using ab initio thermodynamics. The Computational 2D Materials Database contains 16,000 entries, and 2D materials are expected to enable transistor scaling down to ~1 nm by 2031.

Specialty Materials

Data-driven approaches are also advancing specialty materials. Researchers have developed super-adhesive hydrogels for underwater environments by mining protein databases and optimizing formulations from 180 bioinspired hydrogels. The resulting materials achieved adhesive strengths exceeding 1 MPa. The team analyzed a dataset of 24,707 adhesive proteins from 3,822 organisms, selecting the top 200 species for analysis and deriving 180 unique compositions for hydrogel synthesis.

The Northwestern megalibrary used to discover the iridium replacement catalyst has also proven effective for discovering quantum dots and other nanomaterials. Rainbow, the multi-robot laboratory at NC State, is specifically designed to accelerate quantum dot discovery and optimization.

Market Validation: $120M Bets on AI Materials

Capital is flowing into AI materials discovery, signaling confidence that the technology is moving from lab to market.

  • NSF and Intel are investing $20 million over five years to establish the Artificial Intelligence Materials Institute at Cornell University. The institute aims to accelerate materials discovery for sustainable energy and quantum technologies by integrating AI with materials science. Partner institutions include Princeton University, City College of the City University of New York, the Advanced Science Research Center at CUNY, and Boston University. Eun-Ah Kim will serve as director.

  • CuspAI, a British startup, is in talks to raise over $100 million to use artificial intelligence models for discovering new materials. Venture capital firm NEA is set to co-lead the funding round. The investment aims to accelerate AI-driven material discovery for applications including energy and electronics.

  • The broader AI in materials discovery market is showing strong growth. Precedence Research projects significant expansion as industries adopt AI-powered tools for materials design and discovery.

  • Princeton University was tapped as a partner in the new NSF-funded AI materials institute announced in July, further expanding the national network of research institutions focused on AI-accelerated materials science.

Reality Check: AI’s Scientific Limitations

Despite the progress, AI models have significant limitations in scientific reasoning. A new benchmark called MaCBench, introduced in Nature Machine Intelligence on August 11, reveals that even the best multimodal AI models struggle with spatial reasoning and cross-modal synthesis. The benchmark contains 779 multiple-choice questions and 374 numeric-answer questions covering chemistry and materials science tasks.

The results show that while models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Llama 3.2 90B Vision excel at basic perception—achieving 0.77 average accuracy for recognizing laboratory equipment—they perform much worse on reasoning tasks. The models achieved only 0.46 average accuracy for reasoning about laboratory scenarios and 0.53 average accuracy for extracting compositions from tables. These findings suggest that advances in training data and methods are needed before multimodal AI can serve as reliable scientific assistants.

The gap between laboratory discovery and industrial application remains another challenge. In May 2025, NREL convened the ARROWS workshop, bringing together over 50 leaders in AI, materials science, and robotics to discuss how autonomous science can bridge the “valley of death” for new materials. As reported by NREL , the goal is to create intelligent, integrated systems that produce “born-qualified” materials ready for industrial scale from the start.

Workshop organizer Steven R. Spurgeon of NREL, pioneer Sergei V. Kalinin of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and Nathan Park of IBM Research discussed approaches including AI reward functions, causal models, agent-based AI models, modular workflows, and standardized data platforms. The challenge isn’t just discovering materials—it’s ensuring that discovered materials can be manufactured at scale and integrated into existing industrial processes.

What This Means

The pattern from August’s developments is clear: AI has moved from augmenting materials scientists to partially automating discovery. The Northwestern catalyst discovered in one afternoon, Rainbow’s 1,000 daily experiments, and foundation models trained on billions of molecules all point to the same shift—from serendipitous discovery to targeted design, from intuition-driven exploration to data-driven optimization.

The $120 million in funding announcements this month suggests that investors and government agencies see the potential for commercial impact. The autonomous labs moving from research prototypes to commercial facilities at Chemify and being open-sourced by NIST indicate that the technology is maturing.

But the MaCBench results and the NREL workshop provide important perspective. AI models still struggle with spatial reasoning and complex scientific tasks. The path from laboratory discovery to industrial product remains long and uncertain. The transformation underway is real, but it’s gradual rather than revolutionary.

The most successful organizations will likely be those that combine AI acceleration with human expertise—using autonomous labs for high-throughput screening, foundation models for prediction, and human scientists for hypothesis generation, interpretation, and application knowledge. The iridium replacement discovered at Northwestern wasn’t found by AI alone; it was found by researchers who knew exactly what problem they needed to solve and had built a tool capable of solving it.

That combination—clear problem definition, AI-accelerated exploration, and scientific expertise—is what will determine whether AI materials discovery fulfills its promise.

Autonomous Labs: From Research to Reality

NIST AFL Not specified Fluid formulations Open source
Chemifarm (Chemify) Not specified Drug and materials discovery Commercial (21,500 sq ft)

item.title: Quantum Computing in August: Error Correction Breakthroughs, 10,000-Qubit Ambitions, and Growing Scientific Debate
item.description:
IBM unveiled a decoder that achieves “orders of magnitude” better error correction, Fujitsu launched a bold 10,000-qubit roadmap targeting 2030, and a corrected paper rekindled controversy over Microsoft’s $1 billion Majorana qubit program. Meanwhile, the industry accelerated toward practical quantum computing with new partnerships, product launches, and enterprise adoption.

This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published during August 2025, surveying the latest developments across error correction breakthroughs, scaling roadmaps, scientific debate, research advances, product launches, and industry maturation.
